source_text: Ἐπὶ τῇ ἄλλῃ πάσῃ φιλοπονίᾳ καὶ σπουδῇ, τὴν περὶ θεολογίας διδασκαλίαν καὶ εὐλάβειαν πῶς ἂν ἐξέλθοιμι τῷ λόγῳ, εἰς αὐτὴν τὴν διάθεσιν εἰσδὺς τοῦ ἀνδρός, σὺν οἵᾳ γνώμῃ καὶ παρασκευῇ τοὺς περὶ τοῦ θείου πάντας ἐκμανθάνειν ἡμᾶς ἤθελε λόγους, φυλαττόμενος μή πῃ κινδυνεύσαιμεν περὶ τὸ ἀναγκαιότατον ἁπάντων, τὴν τοῦ πάντων αἰτίου γνῶσιν; φιλοσοφεῖν μὲν γὰρ ἠξίου, ἀναλεγομένους τῶν ἀρχαίων πάντα ὅσα καὶ φιλοσόφων καὶ ὑμνῳδῶν ἐστι γράμματα πάσῃ δυνάμει, μηδὲν ἐκποιουμένους, μηδ' ἀποδοκιμάζοντας (οὐδέπω γὰρ οὐδὲ τὴν κρίσιν ἔχειν ἐδυνάμεθα), πλὴν ὅσα τῶν ἀθέων εἴη, ὅσοι ἐκκυλισθέντες ὁμοῦ καὶ τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων ἐννοιῶν, οὐκ εἶναι Θεὸν ἢ πρόνοιαν λέγουσι· ταῦτα γὰρ οὔτ' ἀναγινώσκειν ἄξιον, ἵνα μηδ' ἐν τῷ τυχόντι μολύνοιθ' ἡμῖν ἡ ψυχή, εὐσεβεῖν μέλλουσα, λόγων δὲ ἀκούουσα ὑπεναντίων τῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ θεραπείᾳ· οὐδὲ γὰρ τοὺς τοῖς ναοῖς προσιόντας, εὐσεβείας εἶναι οἴονται, ἐφάπτεσθαί τινος ὅλως τῶν βεβήλων. τὰ τούτων τοίνυν οὐδ' ὅλως οὐδὲ ἀριθμεῖσθαι ἄξιον παρ' ἀνδράσιν εὐσεβεῖν ἐπανελομένοις· τοῖς δὲ λοιποῖς πᾶσιν ἐντυγχάνειν καὶ προσομιλεῖν, γένος μὲν οὐδὲ ἕν, οὐδὲ λόγον φιλόσοφον προτιμήσαντας, οὔτε αὖ ἀποδοκιμάσαντας, οὔτε Ἑλληνικὸν οὔτε βάρβαρον, πάντων δὲ ἀκούοντας. σοφῶς τοῦτο καὶ μάλα ἐντέχνως· μή πῃ εἷς τις καὶ καθ' ἑαυτὸν τῶνδέ τινων ἢ τῶνδε λόγος, αὐτὸς μόνος ἀκουσθεὶς καὶ τιμηθείς, κἂν μὴ ἀληθινὸς ὢν τύχῃ, ὡς μόνος ἀληθὴς ὤν, εἰσδὺς εἰς τὴν ψυχὴν ἡμῶν ἐξαπατήσῃ, καὶ καθ' ἑαυτὸν διαθεὶς ἰδίους ἡμᾶς ποιήσηται, οὐκέτ' ἀποστῆναι δυναμένους, οὐδὲ ἀποπλύνασθαι, ὥσπερ τὰ δευσοποιόν τινα βαφὴν βαφέντα τῶν ἐρίων. δεινόν τε γὰρ χρῆμα καὶ εὔστροφον λόγος ὁ ἀνθρώπων, ποικίλος τε τοῖς σοφίσμασι, καὶ ὀξὺς εἰσδραμὼν εἰς τὰς ἀκοάς, τυπῶσαί τε τὸν νοῦν καὶ προθέσθαι, καὶ ἀναπείσας τοὺς ἅπαξ ἁρπασθέντας, ὡς ἀληθὴς ἀγαπᾶσθαι, καὶ μένειν ἔνδον, κἂν ψευδὴς καὶ ἀπατηλὸς ᾖ, ὥσπερ τις γόης κρατῶν, ὑπέρμαχον ἔχων αὐτὸν τὸν ἠπατημένον. εὐεξαπάτητόν τε πάλιν ὑπὸ λόγου καὶ εὔκολον πρὸς συγκατάθεσιν ψυχὴ ἀνθρώπου, ἑτοίμη τε, πρὶν διακρίνῃ καὶ ἐξετάσῃ πάντα τρόπον, ὑπὸ ἀμβλύτητος καὶ ἀσθενείας τῆς ἰδίας, ἢ ὑπὸ λεπτότητος τῆς τοῦ λόγου πρὸς τὴν ἀκρίβειαν τῆς ἐξετάσεως ἀποκαμοῦσαν, ἑαυτὴν ἀπραγμονέστερον παραδιδόναι πολλάκις ψευδέσι λόγοις καὶ δόγμασι, πεπλανημένοις μὲν αὐτοῖς, πλανῶσι δὲ καὶ τοὺς ἐσχηκότας· καὶ οὐ τοῦτο μόνον, ἀλλὰ κἂν ἐπανορθοῦν ἕτερος ἐθέλοι λόγος, οὐκέτι προσιεμένη οὐδὲ μεταπειθομένη, τοῦ δὲ ἐν αὐτῇ περιεχομένη, ὥσπερ τινὸς τυράννου ἀπαραιτήτου αὐτῆς κεκρατηκότος.
thought_title: Read every writer except those who deny God
orientation: Origen had them read every philosopher and poet except those who deny God, so that no single doctrine would hold them captive.
pass_a_gloss: In addition to all the other love of labor and zeal, how could I go through in speech the teaching about theology and the reverent caution, having entered into the very disposition of the man: with what judgment and preparation he wished us to learn thoroughly all the discourses about the divine, guarding lest somehow we be in danger concerning the most necessary of all, the knowledge of the Cause of all? For he thought it right to philosophize, gathering up / reading of the ancients all the writings there are of philosophers and of hymn-singers with all power, putting away nothing, rejecting nothing, except whatever belonged to the atheists, who, having rolled out together also from human notions, say that there is not God or providence. For these it is not worthy even to read, so that not even in the slightest our soul might be defiled, being about to be pious, but hearing words contrary to the service/worship of God. For not even those approaching the temples do they think it of piety to touch anything at all of the profane. The things of these, then, are not worthy at all even to be counted among men who have taken up piety. But with all the rest to meet with and converse, preferring not even one kind/school, nor philosophical doctrine, nor again rejecting, neither Greek nor barbarian, but hearing all. Wisely this and very skilfully: lest somehow some one doctrine by itself of these or those, alone heard and honored, even if it happen not to be true, as being alone true, entering into our soul should deceive us, and having disposed us after itself make us its own, no longer able to stand away nor wash out, like wool dyed with a fast dye. For human speech/argument is a formidable thing and versatile, varied with sophisms, and sharp at running into the ears, to stamp the mind and set itself before it, and, having persuaded those once seized, to be loved as true and to remain within, even if false and deceptive, like some sorcerer in power, having as champion the deceived man himself. And again easily deceived by argument and easy toward assent is the soul of man, and ready, before it discerns and examines in every way, from its own dullness and weakness, or having grown weary by the subtlety of the argument toward the exactness of the examination, to hand itself over rather carelessly often to false arguments and doctrines, themselves led astray and leading astray those who hold them; and not this only, but even if another argument should wish to correct it, no longer admitting nor being persuaded over, but clinging to the one in it, as if some inexorable tyrant had mastered it.

pass_b_english: Beyond all his other diligence and zeal, how could I set out in words his teaching on theology and the reverent care he brought to it? How could I enter into the man's very disposition and show with what judgment and what preparation he wanted us to learn thoroughly all that has been said about the divine, taking care that we should never run into danger over the most necessary thing of all, the knowledge of the Cause of all things? For he thought it right that we should study philosophy by reading, with all our strength, every writing of the ancients, whether philosophers or poets, setting nothing aside and rejecting nothing, since we were not yet able even to judge, except the writings of the atheists, who have fallen away even from the common notions of humankind and say that there is no God and no providence. These are not worth reading, so that our soul, which is meant to be devout, should not be stained even slightly by hearing words opposed to the worship of God. After all, people do not think it fitting to piety for those who go up to the temples to touch anything profane at all. The books of such men, then, are not worth even counting among people who have chosen to live devoutly. But all the rest he wanted us to read and engage with, preferring no single school or philosophical doctrine and rejecting none, whether Greek or barbarian, but listening to them all. This was wise and very skillful. He did not want some one teaching of this party or that, heard and honored by itself alone, to slip into our soul as the only truth, even if it should happen not to be true, and so deceive us, shaping us to itself and making us its own, so that we could no longer break away from it or wash it out, like wool dyed with a dye that will not run. For human argument is a formidable and supple thing, intricate with its sophistries and quick to rush into the ears, to stamp the mind and fix itself there; and once it has persuaded those it has seized, it is loved as true and stays inside, even if it is false and deceitful, like a sorcerer in control, with the very man it has deceived as its champion. And the human soul in turn is easily deceived by argument and quick to give its assent. Before it has weighed and tested a thing in every way, it is often ready, through its own dullness and weakness, or because the subtlety of the argument has made it weary of testing it closely, to hand itself over too easily to false arguments and doctrines, which are themselves astray and lead astray those who hold them. And not only that: even if another argument should want to set it right, it no longer admits it or lets itself be persuaded, but clings to the one already within it, as though some tyrant deaf to every plea had mastered it.
notes: Copy-text: 1622 Paris Greek column as given in the source row (printed pp. 69-70). ὑμνῳδοί ('hymn-singers') are the poets, rendered 'poets'. The print reads εὐσεβείας εἶναι οἴονται; translated as printed: the accusative τοὺς … προσιόντας is the subject of ἐφάπτεσθαι, so 'people do not think it fitting to piety for those who go up to the temples to touch anything profane'; Koetschau's εὐσεβείας, ἧς οἴονται would give 'those who approach the temples of the piety they believe in', with the same point. The print adds ἐδυνάμεθα ('we were not yet able even to judge'), translated. ἐκποιουμένους rendered 'setting nothing aside'. προθέσθαι (ligature unclear in the scan) rendered 'fix itself there'. No Scripture quoted or clearly alluded to in this section.
